## 📖 Overview of WebGL *(from your course notes)*

With the rise of HTML5, browsers evolved into sophisticated application platforms, creating a need for built-in 3D graphics. WebGL was designed to fill that role — often described as *"OpenGL for web browsers."*

**Key advantages of WebGL (from your notes):**
- No special plug-ins or libraries needed — it's built into the browser
- Cross-platform
- Uses familiar HTML and JavaScript alongside 3D graphics code
- Enables rich UIs, 3D games, and data visualization
- Only needs a text editor and browser to develop
- Published using standard web technologies

---

## 🌐 Additional context from the web *(outside course material)*

<cite index="1-1">WebGL is a JavaScript API for rendering high-performance interactive 3D and 2D graphics within any compatible web browser without the use of plug-ins.</cite>

<cite index="1-2">It does so by introducing an API that closely conforms to OpenGL ES 2.0, usable in HTML `<canvas>` elements.</cite> <cite index="1-5">This conformance makes it possible for the API to take advantage of hardware graphics acceleration provided by the user's device.</cite>

<cite index="1-7">WebGL 2 introduces support for much of the OpenGL ES 3.0 feature set, provided through the `WebGL2RenderingContext` interface.</cite>

---

## 🖊️ The OpenGL ES Shading Language (GLSL ES) *(from your course notes)*

The language used to write shaders is called a **shading language**. Since WebGL is based on OpenGL ES 2.0, it uses **GLSL ES** for creating shaders. This means WebGL pages are built with **three languages**:
1. **HTML5** — structure
2. **JavaScript** — logic/control
3. **GLSL ES** — shader code

---

## 🌐 Additional context from the web *(outside course material)*

<cite index="3-3">WebGL programs consist of control code written in JavaScript and shader code (GLSL) that is executed on a computer's Graphics Processing Unit (GPU).</cite>

<cite index="7-15,7-16">Shaders use GLSL — a special OpenGL shading language with syntax similar to C — executed directly by the graphics pipeline. They split into **vertex shaders** (transform shape positions to 3D coordinates) and **fragment shaders** (compute rendering colors and other attributes).</cite>

<cite index="17-1">The WebGL shading language is a restricted variant of the OpenGL ES Shading Language 1.00, enabling flexible shading and some general purpose usage of GPUs on the web.</cite>
